title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Priya Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards for APIs, code, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also records key Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) that govern platform-wide choices. Use this as the canonical reference for design reviews, PR checklists, onboarding, and audits.

Sections
1) API Standards
2) Coding Standards
3) Infrastructure (Infra) Standards
4) Model-Serving Standards
5) Observability Standards
6) Performance Standards and SLOs
7) ADRs (selected)
8) Rollout & Change Procedures
9) Ownership & Escalation

1) API Standards
Short intro: All external-facing and internal HTTP APIs must be designed for clarity, versionability, and automated compatibility checks. Wherever possible APIs should be OpenAPI v3-described and contract-tested.

Key rules:
- Specification: Every service must provide an OpenAPI v3 spec in the repo at /openapi/openapi.yaml. Specs are the source of truth for SDK generation and client integrations.
- Versioning: Use major-version URI prefix for breaking changes, e.g. /v1/embedding or /v2/generation. Deprecation window: minimum 90 days for hosted API; notify customers and provide migration guide.
- Naming & Resources: Use nouns for resources and clear sub-resources, e.g. POST /v1/models/{model_id}/invocations, GET /v1/models/{model_id}/metrics. Avoid verbs in the path.
- Idempotency: All resource-creating endpoints must support client-supplied idempotency keys (Idempotency-Key header). Retries must be safe for transient errors.
- Authentication/Authorization: Use Bearer tokens from Redwood IAM. Token scopes must be documented in the OpenAPI securitySchemes. For internal services use mTLS between clusters and short-lived JWTs for workload-to-workload calls.
- Pagination: Use cursor-based pagination for large lists (limit + next_cursor).
- Error model: Standardize on problem+json (RFC 7807) for errors. Include: type, title, status, request_id, and a machine-readable code (e.g., "MODEL_NOT_READY").
- Request/Response size limits: Default request payload <= 2 MB for non-streaming APIs. Streaming endpoints (chunked responses) can exceed this but must document per-model token limits.
- Rate limiting & Quotas: Per-API tier limits applied at the API gateway (inference-router). Standard hosted tier: 100 req/min per API key with burst allowance + queueing; Dedicated tiers are configured per-contract.
- Contract testing: CI must run a contract test that validates the OpenAPI schema against a running service (tooling: pact/openapi-validator).

Example OpenAPI snippet (high-level):

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Redwood Inference API
  version: 'v1'
paths:
  /v1/models/{model_id}/invocations:
    post:
      summary: Synchronous generation
      parameters:
        - name: model_id
          in: path
          required: true
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerationRequest'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: successful response
```

2) Coding Standards
Goal: Maintainable, testable, and secure code with fast code review cycles.

Language & style:
- Primary backend languages: Go (services with latency-sensitive paths), Python (ML helpers, evals), and TypeScript (console + SDK).
- Enforce formatting: gofmt/gomod for Go, black + isort for Python, prettier + eslint for TypeScript.
- Linting: Each repo must have a CI lint step (golangci-lint, pylint/ruff, eslint).

Testing:
- Unit tests: target >70% coverage for core business logic.
- Integration tests: Exercised in CI against ephemeral infra or service mocks.
- Contract/Schema tests: see API Standards.
- Performance tests: Critical slow-paths (inference-router, batcher, kv-cache) require automated perf checks in the perf-suite.

PR/process:
- PRs require at least one approving review from the owning team and passing CI. For changes impacting infra or SLOs, include owners from eng-platform or eng-sre as reviewers.
- Commit messages: Conventional commits (type(scope): subject). Use squashed merges for feature branches.
- Tracing & feature flags: All long-running operations must emit trace spans and be behind a feature flag when behavior is experimental.

Secrets & scanning:
- No secrets in code. Use Vault/KMS. Pre-commit hooks scan for accidental secrets.

3) Infrastructure (Infra) Standards
Scope: Terraform & IaC, cloud accounts, networking, and packaging for Private deployments.

Terraform & modules:
- Use top-level, audited terraform modules in git::ssh://git@company/infra/modules. Modules must have CHANGELOG.md and documented inputs/outputs.
- State: remote state stored in encrypted S3 with DynamoDB locking (AWS) or equivalent. Avoid local state.
- Environments: dev/staging/prod workspace separation. Changes to prod require plan review and approval from infra-owners.

Cloud & networking:
- Region policy: Primary regions: us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1. Private deployments must surface supported-region matrix.
- VPC & subnets: All deployments must use dedicated VPCs per-customer for private mode. Subnets follow the standard naming convention: <team>-<env>-subnet-<az>.
- KMS/HSM: Customer secrets must be stored in KMS-backed secrets stores; HSM integration for enterprise customers on request.

Tagging & cost attribution:
- Every resource must include tags: {team, env, cost_center, project, owner}. Reporting jobs run nightly to assert tagging compliance.

Disaster recovery & backups:
- Critical stateful components (db, keystore, model-repo indexes) must have nightly snapshots and documented RTO/RPO.

4) Model-Serving Standards
Scope: Model packaging, variants, quantization profiles, routing, and rollout policies.

Model packaging & versioning:
- Models are versioned semantically: <model-name>-v<major>.<minor> (e.g., redwood-open-7b-v1.2). Model artifacts must include manifest.json with architecture, tokenizer, sequence_length, kv_cache_compatibility, and known performance profile (latency/tokens/sec).
- Quantization profiles are codified under /quantization-profiles with keys: fp16, int8, int4 and recommended hardware.

Serving patterns:
- Components: inference-router, model-orchestrator, batcher, kv-cache, and tracer.
- Prefix/KV caching: Implement prefix-based KV caching for conversational workloads; cache key constructed as model_id|conversation_id|prefix_hash. Cache TTL default: 1 hour, configurable per-route.
- Batching: Batching is automatic in runtime; per-route batch size limit must be configured (recommended default 32 for small models, 8 for L4 NVLink setups).

Rollouts & fallback:
- Canary releases: 5% -> 20% -> 60% -> 100% traffic with metric gates at each step (error rate, p95 latency, quality regression). Canary windows: minimum 30 minutes at each step unless explicitly extended.
- Fallback variants: Services must register compatible fallback models (e.g., 7B-fast-quantized fallback for 7B-fp16) and an automated policy that routes to fallback on capacity or degraded SLOs.

Quality monitoring:
- Each model deployment must be associated with an eval-suite (prompt sets + expected outputs). Continuous quality checks run on a daily cadence and can trigger regression alerts.

5) Observability Standards
Objective: Detect SLO violations quickly and provide actionable context for remediation.

Metrics taxonomy (per-service):
- request_total (labels: service, route, model_id, status_code)
- request_latency_seconds (histogram)
- token_generated_total (labels: service, model_id)
- cache_hit_total / cache_miss_total (labels: route, model_id)
- batching_size_distribution (histogram)

SLOs & alerts (see Performance below). Alerting principles:
- Pager only for actionable, urgent incidents. Use Slack/ops channels for informational alerts.
- All alerts must include: symptoms, runbook link, recent traces, and affected services.
- Tracing: Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) required across RPC boundaries with consistent trace IDs injected in request_id header. Sampler default: 10% global, 100% for errors and high-latency traces.

Logging:
- Structured logs JSON with keys: timestamp, service, env, level, request_id, model_id, route, message, extra. Logs must avoid PII and sensitive customer data.

Dashboards:
- Per-service dashboard template: traffic, latency (p50/p95/p99), error rate, token cost breakdown, cache stats, and infra utilization. Dashboards are templated in Grafana and created via repo automation.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs
High-level SLOs (hosted API defaults, Dedicated can be contracted):
- Availability: 99.95% uptime (rolling 30d) for hosted API control plane and 99.9% for model-serving endpoints under normal load.
- Latency (generation endpoints):
  - p50 <= 120 ms for small low-latency models (e.g., optimized 2-3B variants)
  - p95 <= 400 ms for typical generation requests (short prompts, <= 256 tokens)
  - p99 <= 1.5 s for same profile; longer sequences have proportional expectations
- Throughput: measured in tokens/sec per-GPU; each model profile must state tokens/sec at batch sizes 1, 8, 32 on supported hardware.

Error budgets & escalation:
- Error budget computed daily. If burn rate > 2x for 24h, escalate to on-call + SRE/Platform review. Post-incident actions: incident review + remediation plan within 5 business days if allocation exceeded.

Perf testing:
- Every change that touches the runtime, batcher, or kernels must run against the benchmarking-and-perf-suite with documented baseline regression thresholds. A CI gate blocks merges on >3% regression in p95 latency for affected scenarios.

7) ADRs (selected)
ADR-2026-01: Standardize on OpenAPI v3 for external and internal HTTP APIs
- Context: Multiple teams shipped divergent API styles leading to SDK fragmentation and brittle integrations.
- Decision: Mandate OpenAPI v3 as canonical contract for HTTP services. Include securitySchemes and example responses.
- Consequences: Requires updating legacy services; added CI contract-tests.
- Owners: eng-developer-experience, eng-platform.

ADR-2026-02: Use Go for latency-sensitive control plane paths; Python for model tooling and evals
- Context: Need clear language division to optimize for performance and developer productivity.
- Decision: Adopt Go for high-throughput RPC endpoints (inference-router, kv-cache), Python for ML-heavy components and eval harness.
- Consequences: Establish language-specific infra (gRPC codegen for Go; Python wheels for tooling).

ADR-2026-03: Default quantization profile set and fallback policy
- Decision: Default hosted models use fp16 where available; int8-int4 quantized variants recommended for Dedicated/private to save cost. Runtime will expose a fallback routing policy to move traffic to quantized variants on capacity strain.

8) Rollout & Change Procedures
Standard rollout (service or model change):
1. Create design doc and link to PR. Include expected impact on SLOs, infra, and cost.
2. Run unit and contract tests in CI.
3. Execute automated perf-suite; attach results to PR.
4. Deploy to staging; run smoke tests and daily evals for model changes.
5. Canary in prod (5/20/60/100) with metric gates: error_rate < baseline + 0.5% and p95 latency <= baseline * 1.15 and no eval regression.
6. If any gate fails, roll back to previous variant and open an incident if necessary.

Emergency rollback:
- On severe production degradation, call the on-call engineer and execute the documented rollback runbook for the service or model. For model-serving, route traffic to named fallback variant and scale up capacity where feasible.

9) Ownership & Escalation
- Service owners: each service repo must include CODEOWNERS and an OWNERS.md listing primary and secondary on-call.
- Incident escalation: follow oncall_and_incident_response/incident-process. SRE and Platform teams are first escalation for infra and global SLOs.
